MSK-Skin · Week 14 · Lecture 9

The Basics of Musculoskeletal Imaging

Dr. Brandon Bentley · Full Illustrated Lecture Companion · 68-slide primary source

← Week 14Condensed Factoid →X-ray ABCDsFracturesViewsMRICTCases
Central learning goal: Select the imaging modality that answers the clinical question and read radiographs systematically. The six clinical cases show how an X-ray-first approach can lead to MRI or CT when needed.

1 · Learning objectives and modality map

Dr. Bentley’s six objectives are to understand imaging modalities and indications, recognize normal anatomy, select appropriate views, use an organized interpretation approach, and identify common disease patterns.

ModalityStrengths / indications emphasizedLimits / key principle
X-rayFirst-line for bone, most suspected fractures, many foreign bodies, calcific tendinopathy and arthritis2-dimensional projection; overlapping anatomy means multiple views matter
MRILigament, tendon, cartilage, meniscus, soft-tissue internal derangement; occult fracture and bone stress responseMagnetic field / RF; evaluate device and metal safety before scanning
CTDetailed cortical bone, occult or complex fractures, structures hidden on plain radiographs; CT arthrogramUses ionizing X-ray radiation; typically not preferred to MRI for routine soft tissue injuries
Core decision: Start with the clinical question and a suitable initial X-ray series. Escalate to MRI when occult marrow/soft-tissue injury is the question; choose CT for detailed bony morphology or selected MRI-limited cases.

2 · Plain radiography and the ABCDs

An X-ray uses electromagnetic radiation with differential absorption: dense bone absorbs more and looks radiopaque/white; air and lower-density material appear relatively radiolucent/darker. Calcifications and some foreign bodies are conspicuous.

StepWhat to check
A — Adequacy and AlignmentCorrect study? Adequately includes area of interest? Are adjacent bones congruent? Is there dislocation, subluxation, or abnormal axis?
B — BonesTrace every cortex; assess lucencies, breaks, density, osteopenia, or destructive lesions
C — CartilageJoint spaces serve as radiographic surrogates for cartilage thickness; assess narrowing and alignment
D — Disc/joint space and soft tissuesLook for effusion, swelling, displacement of fat pads, calcification and radiopaque foreign bodies

The slide labels its final check “Soft Tissue,” so remember soft tissue findings even when the acronym is taught with different letters.

3 · Report a fracture in a reproducible way

Use the same sequence every time: (1) bone, (2) location, (3) fracture pattern, (4) fragment relationship/alignment; then note whether open/closed or intra-articular when known.

TermDefinition / cue
Closed vs openOpen communicates with outside through skin; do not infer from imaging alone without examination
Non-displaced vs displacedFragment position relative to original anatomy; lecture mentions minimally displaced ≤3 mm
Angulation / rotation / shortening / appositionDescribe misalignment, rotation, shortening and cortical contact; assess on perpendicular views
Simple / comminuted / segmentalOne break vs multiple fragments; segmental has 2 separated fracture lines isolating a segment
Transverse / oblique / spiralPerpendicular, diagonal or twisting/helical fracture trajectory
AvulsionTendon or ligament traction removes a bone fragment
Intra-articularFracture line extends into joint surface
Impacted / compression / pathologicAxial collapse, compression deformation, or fracture in weakened bone
Reporting practice: “Distal radius fracture, extra-articular, transverse, dorsally angulated and mildly displaced.” A complete description is more useful than simply saying “broken wrist.”

4 · Which radiographic views are useful?

Obtain images at multiple angles—usually orthogonal views—because a fracture or dislocation may be apparent on one projection but hidden on another.

RegionNamed views from the lecture
ShoulderAP; lateral/scapular Y; modified trauma axial; Garth; Zanca; West Point; Grashey
WristPA; oblique; lateral; carpal tunnel; clenched fist
KneeAP; lateral; Merchant/sunrise; weightbearing; Rosenberg
AnkleAP; mortise; lateral; AP stress; horizontal-beam lateral

Recognition first: AP/PA, lateral and oblique are the default orientation concepts; special views answer questions about specific joints/regions. The lecture lists special names without requiring their detailed positioning techniques.

5 · MRI: tissue contrast, sequences and anatomy

MRI aligns hydrogen protons in a strong magnetic field; radiofrequency excitation and signal during realignment provide tissue contrast. It is excellent for ligaments, tendons, menisci, labrum, marrow edema and occult injuries that can be missed on radiographs.

SequenceAppearance emphasizedPractical mnemonic
T1Fat bright; water relatively darkT1 highlights anatomy/fat
T2Water/fluid bright; fat may also be bright without fat suppressionT2 often highlights pathology/edema

The lecture shows coronal, sagittal, and axial images of the shoulder, knee and wrist. Use bony landmarks to orient the plane before identifying tendons/ligaments. MRI is not generally first-line; verify the MRI safety status of implants or foreign bodies rather than assuming every implanted device precludes it (current-practice qualification).

6 · CT: when bony detail is the priority

Computed tomography combines many radiographic projections to reconstruct cross-sectional and multiplanar images. It helps characterize complex fracture geometry, intra-articular involvement and cortical bone injury obscured by superimposition on X-ray. The lecture also mentions CT arthrography and use when MRI cannot be obtained.

Contrast the strengths: MRI excels at marrow and soft tissues; CT depicts cortical bone, fragment detail and complex articular surfaces very well. Both may help clarify an occult fracture in specific situations.

7 · Six lecture cases: the imaging decision

PresentationInitial imagingNext / definitive answer
67-year-old with chronic activity-related knee painWeightbearing knee radiographsAssess joint-space narrowing and degenerative changes; no reflex MRI for uncomplicated suspected OA
23-year-old with pivot, pop and immediate effusionPlain knee radiographsMRI assesses suspected ACL rupture/soft tissues; slide 53 labels absent ACL
FOOSH, anatomic snuffbox tenderness, negative first filmsWrist/scaphoid radiographsThumb-spica immobilization and repeat films ~2 weeks as presented; MRI if still suspicious; CT for fracture detail/healing
Overhead exercise / lateral shoulder painShoulder radiographsMRI can assess suspected rotator cuff / soft tissue problem when indicated
Recurrent shoulder dislocation/subluxationShoulder radiographsCT depicts bony defects; Hill–Sachs (humeral head) and Bankart (glenoid rim) illustrated
Runner, progressive tibial activity painPlain X-rays firstMRI best grades early bone stress reaction and marrow abnormalities
Lecture-specific note: These are slide-based teaching examples, not a universal imaging-order algorithm. For scaphoid injury, expedited MRI or CT may be selected in modern practice rather than waiting two weeks.

8 · Retrieval checkpoints

Which modality is first-line for most suspected fractures and why?

Plain radiographs; quick, effective cortical bone assessment, and they can guide advanced imaging selection.

What is the ABCD interpretation approach?

Adequacy/alignment, bones, cartilage/joint space, and adjacent soft tissue/disc findings.

How do you distinguish T1 from T2?

T1: fat bright. T2: water/fluid bright; without suppression, fat may also be bright.

Why do you need 2 views for angulation?

A deformity hidden by one projection may become apparent on the perpendicular view.

What image next for acute pivot with pop, effusion and suspected ACL injury?

Radiographs initially; MRI to evaluate suspected ACL disruption.

What if snuffbox tenderness persists with a normal initial X-ray?

Protect/immobilize presumed occult scaphoid injury; the lecture uses repeat X-rays and MRI if suspicion persists.

Which should you choose for complex bony architecture vs stress reaction?

CT for detailed complex fractures; MRI for an early stress reaction that may be X-ray occult.
